name: Marcomanni
info: The Marcomanni were a Suebian Germanic people beside the Roman Danube frontier, recorded from 58 BCE to about 400 CE, remembered for the Bohemian kingdom of Maroboduus and the Marcomannic Wars against Marcus Aurelius.

facts.capital: Buiaimon, the royal seat of Maroboduus in Boiohaemum (Bohemia), by Strabo's account
facts.founder: not known; Maroboduus founded their kingdom in Boiohaemum
facts.predecessor: The Suebian peoples of the Grossromstedter culture of the middle Elbe and Saale; in Bohemia, the lands of the Boii
facts.successor: Suebian groups that joined the empire of Attila, the Kingdom of the Suebi, the Lombards, the Alemanni and probably the Baiuvarii

t: After a heavy defeat by Drusus the elder around 9 BCE, the Marcomanni moved under King Maroboduus into Boiohaemum, a land the Boii had held, whose name is the origin of Bohemia.
Maroboduus built a Rome-aligned Suebian empire, but his refusal to back the revolt of Arminius in 9 CE split the Germanic peoples, and he was deposed in 19 CE and died in exile at Ravenna.
In the Marcomannic Wars under Marcus Aurelius the Marcomanni and Quadi invaded Italy itself, before Rome stationed 20,000 men in each of their countries by 180.
dyk: Velleius Paterculus wrote that Maroboduus drilled his Bohemian soldiers almost to Roman standards and could call upon 70,000 experienced infantry and 4,000 cavalry.
ev: The Marcomanni fight among the confederates of Ariovistus against Julius Caesar in Gaul
Drusus the elder almost wipes out the Marcomanni in his campaigns in Germania
Maroboduus has established a powerful kingdom in Boiohaemum, which Augustus comes to see as a threat
War breaks out between the Germanic alliances led by Arminius and Maroboduus
Catualda deposes Maroboduus, who goes into exile among the Romans at Ravenna
The Marcomanni and Quadi cross the Danube, destroy Opitergium and besiege Aquileia
The Romans win a decisive battle at Laugaricio, and by 180 the Marcomanni and Quadi are under occupation
The Marcomanni join Huns, Goths, Alans and others in a great raid across the Danube into the Roman Balkans

sections.foundation:
The name Marcomanni probably comes from a Proto-Germanic word reconstructed as *markō, “border”, making them “border men”; which frontier it recalled is unknown. They first appear among the confederates of Ariovistus whom Julius Caesar defeated in Gaul in 58 BCE, drawn up by tribe beside the Harudes, Tribocci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Sedusii and Suebi. Their homeland east of the Rhine is uncertain: one common proposal is the Mainfranken region of northwestern Bavaria, and archaeology links them and their Suebian neighbours with the Grossromstedter culture of the middle Elbe and Saale.

Under Augustus the Romans invaded Germania, and Florus and Orosius report that Drusus the elder almost wiped out the Marcomanni in his campaigns of 12–9 BCE and raised a mound of their spoils. The Marcomanni then moved, under their new king Maroboduus, who had grown up in Rome, into Boiohaemum, plains surrounded by the Hercynian Forest where the Boii had lived. The name is the origin of Bohemia. Tacitus wrote that their territory “was won by valour”, and by 6 BCE Maroboduus had established a powerful kingdom there.
sections.socioeconomy:
Archaeology of the Bohemian settlement, including cremation and inhumation burials, hints at a stratified society that gave special importance to its warrior class. The Plaňany group that developed in the old Boii lands shows the influence of the earlier Celtic La Tène culture, and the wider Grossromstedter culture drew on the Jastorf culture of the central Elbe and the Przeworsk culture of present-day Poland. The Marcomanni are archaeologically hard to tell apart from other Suebian groups such as the Quadi and Hermunduri.

After the fall of Vannius in 50/51 CE the Germanic population just north of the Danube grew, in present-day Lower Austria, Moravia and western Slovakia, and the region received increasing imports from the empire; Slovak archaeologists place a core area of the Vannian kingdom in the fertile lowlands around Trnava. Rome supported their kings with arms and, as Tacitus put it, “more frequently by our money”. Long periods of peace and prosperity alternated with war. After the Marcomannic Wars some Marcomanni were settled in Italy and other parts of the empire, Gallienus settled others in Pannonia Superior, and by the late 4th century at least some had become Christians.
sections.military:
Velleius Paterculus wrote that Maroboduus drilled his soldiers almost to Roman standards and could call on 70,000 experienced infantry and 4,000 cavalry, probably not all Marcomanni, and that Rome feared he might invade Italy. In 6 CE Augustus sent two army groups under Sentius Saturninus and Tiberius against the Marcomanni in a pincer movement, but a revolt in Pannonia stopped the campaign. In 17 CE war broke out between the alliances of Arminius and Maroboduus, and after an indecisive battle Maroboduus withdrew into Bohemia. In 89 Domitian, after killing their peace envoys, was defeated by the Marcomanni.

The Marcomannic Wars under Marcus Aurelius were longer and bloodier. In 167 or 169 the Marcomanni and Quadi crossed the Danube, destroyed Opitergium and besieged Aquileia. Marcus Aurelius made his headquarters at Carnuntum, and in 179 Marcus Valerius Maximianus won a decisive battle at Laugaricio (Trenčín). By 180 Roman garrisons of 20,000 men each were stationed among the Marcomanni and the Quadi. In 395 the Marcomanni crossed the frozen Danube with Huns, Goths, Alans and others, setting their wagons around themselves like a wall as Stilicho approached.
sections.governance:
The Marcomanni were ruled by kings. Tacitus wrote around 100 CE that they and the Quadi had kings of their own nation, descended from the noble stock of Maroboduus and Tudrus, but that their strength depended on Roman influence. Maroboduus, who had lived in Rome and been favoured by Augustus, ruled from his royal seat Buiaimon. By Strabo's account his empire included the Lugii, the Semnones and peoples such as the Zumi, Butones, Mugilones and Sibini, and by 5 CE the Langobardi; Velleius said he subjugated all his neighbours by war or treaty.

Rome sought to control their leaders. After Maroboduus fell, his and Catualda's subjects were moved to land between the Morava and the Cusus rivers under the Quadian king Vannius, who grew rich and unpopular and was overthrown in 50/51; his nephews Vangio and Sido divided his realm as Roman client kings. In the 160s Ballomarius, king of the Marcomanni, led a peace mission to the governor of Pannonia. Gallienus took Pipa, daughter of the Marcomannic king Attalus, as a concubine, and after 395 the Christian queen Fritigil corresponded with Ambrose of Milan, who began a peace treaty with Stilicho.
sections.impact:
The Marcomanni left their mark on the name of Bohemia, through the Germanic Boiohaemum, and for a time their kingdom was the only part of Germania that Rome did not control before the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE. When Arminius sent Maroboduus the head of the defeated general Publius Quinctilius Varus, Maroboduus sent it on to Rome, and his refusal to join the revolt split the Germanic peoples into two warring alliances. The Marcomannic Wars led Marcus Aurelius to consider a new imperial province called Marcomannia, a plan Commodus dropped after his father's death in 180.

Their descendants passed into many peoples. Marcomanni were settled inside the empire and served throughout it: the Notitia Dignitatum of about 420 lists a tribune of the Marcomanni under the dux of northern Noricum and Pannonia I, palatine units of Marcomanni in Italy and Equites Marcomanni in North Africa. Many Suebi, probably including Marcomanni, went west and founded the Kingdom of the Suebi in Gallaecia; others joined the empire of Attila, the Lombards and the Alemanni, and it is very likely that the Baiuvarii included Marcomanni.
sections.decline:
In the 3rd century the centre of Suebian activity on the Danube shifted east, reflecting the rising importance of the Quadi and the decline of the Marcomanni. Caracalla boasted around 214/215 of his enmity with the Marcomanni, Jordanes believed they paid tribute to the Gothic king Ostrogotha, and Diocletian claimed a triumph over them in 299. After the Roman defeat at the Battle of Adrianople in 378 the Goths, Alans and Huns came to dominate the Middle Danube, and the Rugii and Heruli may already have moved into the Marcomanni's old lands.

In 395 the Marcomanni joined the great raid across the Danube, after which Claudian wrote that the lands between the Black Sea and the Adriatic were like deserts. The Notitia Dignitatum of about 420 gives the last clear trace of a Marcomannic polity, probably now south of the Danube. Paulus Diaconus later listed the Marcomanni among the peoples Attila could call upon, though modern scholars doubt they were still distinguished from other Suebi. After Attila's death in 453 a Suebian kingdom under Hunimund and Alaric appeared in or near north-eastern Pannonia.

summary: The Marcomanni were a Suebian Germanic people who settled in Bohemia under King Maroboduus around the turn of the era and lived for four centuries beside Rome's Danube frontier, alternating long periods of peace with wars that peaked in the Marcomannic Wars of Marcus Aurelius. By the 5th century they had passed into the empire, the Hunnic world and later Germanic peoples.
references: Guy Halsall, Barbarian Migration and the Roman West, 376-568 (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
Michael Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars: From the Third Century to Alaric (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
Dennis Green, “The Boii, Bohemia, Bavaria”, in Janine Fries-Knoblach and Heiko Steuer (eds.), The Baiuvarii and Thuringi: An Ethnographic Perspective (Boydell & Brewer, 2014)
Heiko Steuer, “Germanen” aus Sicht der Archäologie: Neue Thesen zu einem alten Thema (De Gruyter, 2021)

pointDescs.-58: The Marcomanni appear among the confederates of Ariovistus defeated by Julius Caesar in Gaul.
pointDescs.-9: Drusus the elder almost wipes out the Marcomanni in his campaigns of 12–9 BCE.
pointDescs.-6: By 6 BCE King Maroboduus has led the Marcomanni into Boiohaemum and established a powerful kingdom there.
pointDescs.6: Maroboduus rules a Suebian empire that includes the Langobardi and Semnones; a Roman pincer attack on it is called off by the Pannonian revolt.
pointDescs.17: War breaks out between the alliances of Arminius and Maroboduus; after an indecisive battle Maroboduus withdraws into Bohemia.
pointDescs.19: Catualda deposes Maroboduus, who goes into exile at Ravenna, and the Romans move his subjects under the Quadian king Vannius.
pointDescs.51: Vannius is overthrown in 50/51 and his realm divided between Vangio and Sido as Roman client kings.
pointDescs.89: Domitian makes war in Pannonia, kills the peace envoys sent to him and is defeated by the Marcomanni.
pointDescs.169: The Marcomanni and Quadi cross the Danube, destroy Opitergium and besiege Aquileia (in 167 or 169).
pointDescs.180: After the decisive Roman victory at Laugaricio in 179, the Marcomanni are under occupation by a Roman garrison of 20,000 men.
pointDescs.299: Diocletian claims a triumph over the Marcomanni, by now overshadowed by the Quadi.
pointDescs.395: The Marcomanni join Huns, Goths, Alans and others in a great raid across the Danube into the Roman Balkans.
pointDescs.430: By about this time the Marcomanni no longer appear as a polity; the Notitia Dignitatum of about 420 is the last clear mention of one.

notes: The article uses BC/AD; the profile writes BCE and plain CE years as the Institute does.
The invasion of Italy is dated 'either in 167 AD ... or in 169 AD' by the article; the event keeps '167 or 169', and the point uses 169.
The date of Drusus's victory is uncertain (12-9 BCE; scholars are not unanimous on 9 BCE); the point at -9 follows the common date the article discusses.
Tacitus says the Boii were 'driven' out and the territory 'won by valour', while the lead says the land had been 'abandoned' by the Boii; the profile says only that the Boii had lived there.
The register's end year 430 is not an event in the article; the last clear polity mention is the Notitia Dignitatum, around 420.
The Christian queen Fritigil's letters are dated by the article only as 'soon after' 395 (Ambrose was bishop to 397).
